items.stem: A regional public-health team wants to measure how many new cases of a condition occur in its population during the coming year. Which measure is most appropriate?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Incidence concerns new events occurring over time.

distractor_rationales.A: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.C: Reliability describes reproducibility of a measurement, not a population frequency measure.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity concerns correspondence between a measurement and its intended state.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is identified when appraising research, not when selecting a measure of new events.

items.stem: A health-service planner needs a measure that describes the number of people currently living with a chronic condition to estimate the burden on ongoing care. Which measure should be used?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Prevalence counts existing cases and is useful for estimating chronic-care burden.

distractor_rationales.A: Incidence concerns new events over time rather than existing cases.
distractor_rationales.B: Reliability is reproducibility, not a count of people with a condition.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity addresses whether a measurement corresponds to its intended state.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design does not measure the burden of existing cases.

items.stem: A learner states that prevalence and incidence can be used interchangeably because both describe a condition in a population. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: They are interchangeable if the condition is chronic.
Incidence concerns new events over time, whereas prevalence counts existing cases.
Incidence measures reproducibility, whereas prevalence measures validity.
Prevalence identifies the study design, whereas incidence compares groups.
They differ only by the source that reports them.

items.correct_answer_rationale: The measures answer different questions: incidence is about new events over time and prevalence about existing cases.

distractor_rationales.A: The supported distinction is based on new versus existing cases, not chronicity.
distractor_rationales.C: Reliability and validity are separate properties of measurements.
distractor_rationales.D: Study-design appraisal is distinct from choosing incidence or prevalence.
distractor_rationales.E: The measures differ in what they count, not merely in reporting source.

items.stem: A public-health instrument gives the same result when repeated under the same conditions. Which property of the instrument has been demonstrated?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Reliability is the reproducibility of a measurement.

distractor_rationales.A: Validity asks how closely the measurement corresponds to its intended state.
distractor_rationales.B: Incidence is a measure of new events over time.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.E: A study design is not a measurement property.

items.stem: Before adopting a measure for a population-health program, a team asks whether its result closely corresponds to the health state the measure is intended to represent. What property is the team assessing?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Validity is how closely a measurement corresponds to the state it is intended to measure.

distractor_rationales.B: Reliability concerns reproducibility rather than correspondence to the intended state.
distractor_rationales.C: Incidence concerns new events over time.
distractor_rationales.D: Prevalence counts existing cases.
distractor_rationales.E: Participant selection is considered when identifying a study design.

items.stem: A screening measure is highly reproducible when repeated, but the team has not established whether it corresponds to the health state it is intended to measure. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The measure is valid because it is reproducible.
The measure must be a randomized trial.
The measure is reliable, but validity has not been established.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Reproducibility supports reliability; reliability alone does not establish validity.

distractor_rationales.A: A reproducible measurement can still be invalid.
distractor_rationales.B: Incidence is a population-health measure of new events, not a measurement property.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases and is not established by reproducibility.
distractor_rationales.D: A randomized trial is a study design, not a conclusion about measurement reproducibility.

items.stem: A physician is critically appraising a paper that reports an association between an exposure and an outcome. What is the most appropriate first step in assessing the paper's methods?

options.text: Assume the association has the same meaning in every design.
Determine incidence without considering the study methods.
Use reproducibility to identify the comparison structure.
Treat prevalence as the study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal should first identify the study design because designs differ in selection, timing, and comparison.

distractor_rationales.B: The meaning of findings must be appraised in light of the study's design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.C: A study's strengths and limitations should not be inferred without first identifying its design.
distractor_rationales.D: Reproducibility is reliability of a measurement, not a way to identify a design.
distractor_rationales.E: Prevalence is a population-health measure, not a study design.

items.stem: A journal club is comparing two observational studies. To distinguish their designs, which set of features should the group examine?

options.text: Only whether the results are reproducible
Only whether the outcome is chronic
How participants were selected, timed, and compared
Only the number of existing cases
Only the number of new events

items.correct_answer_rationale: Study designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.

distractor_rationales.A: Reproducibility addresses reliability of a measurement, not the features that distinguish designs.
distractor_rationales.B: The supported design comparison concerns selection, timing, and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.D: Existing cases describe prevalence, not study design.
distractor_rationales.E: New events describe incidence, not study design.

items.stem: A trainee begins to list the limitations of a study before determining whether it is randomized, cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: First identify the study design and its comparison structure.
Limitations can be inferred without knowing the study design.
Use prevalence to determine whether the study is randomized.
Use incidence to determine whether the study is cross-sectional.
Use reliability alone to determine the study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Study strengths and limitations should not be inferred without first identifying the design and comparison structure.

distractor_rationales.B: The evidence boundary specifically cautions against inferring strengths or limitations before identifying design.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence is not a means of determining study design.
distractor_rationales.D: Incidence is not a means of determining study design.
distractor_rationales.E: Reliability is a measurement property, not a substitute for identifying the design.

items.stem: A population-health team receives reports from a randomized trial, a cross-sectional study, a cohort study, and a case-control study. Before comparing the reports' findings, what should the team recognize?

options.text: All four designs select and compare participants in the same way.
The designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.
Each design measures prevalence rather than incidence.
Each design establishes validity through reproducibility.
Design identification is unnecessary before comparing findings.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Randomized, cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies differ in participant selection, timing, and comparison.

distractor_rationales.A: The designs are distinguished by differences in selection, timing, and comparison.
distractor_rationales.C: Incidence and prevalence are population-health measures, not properties shared by these designs.
distractor_rationales.D: Reproducibility concerns reliability and does not itself establish validity.
distractor_rationales.E: Critical appraisal should identify design before inferring study strengths or limitations.

items.stem: A physician advising a municipal health program is asked which measure would describe newly identified cases of a condition during a defined period. Which measure is most appropriate?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Incidence concerns new events occurring over time.

distractor_rationales.B: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.C: Reliability describes reproducibility of a measurement.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity describes how closely a measurement corresponds to the state it is intended to measure.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is identified when critically appraising research, not when selecting a frequency measure.

items.stem: A community clinic is planning services for people already living with a long-term condition. Which population-health measure best describes the number of existing cases?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population and is useful for estimating chronic-care burden.

distractor_rationales.A: Incidence concerns new events over time rather than existing cases.
distractor_rationales.B: Reliability is reproducibility of a measurement, not a count of cases.
distractor_rationales.C: Validity concerns correspondence between a measurement and its intended state.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design does not describe the number of existing cases.

items.stem: During a public-health briefing, a learner proposes using incidence and prevalence interchangeably. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Incidence concerns new events over time; prevalence counts existing cases.
Prevalence concerns new events over time; incidence counts existing cases.
The measures are distinguished by study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Incidence and prevalence address different population-health questions: new events over time versus existing cases.

distractor_rationales.A: Existing cases are counted by prevalence, not both measures.
distractor_rationales.B: Reproducibility refers to reliability, not incidence or prevalence.
distractor_rationales.D: This reverses the supported definitions of incidence and prevalence.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is a separate consideration in critical appraisal.

items.stem: A public-health questionnaire produces the same result when it is repeated under the same conditions. Which property has been demonstrated?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Reliability is the reproducibility of a measurement.

distractor_rationales.A: Incidence is a measure of new events over time.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity concerns correspondence to the state the measure is intended to represent.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is not a property of a measurement.

items.stem: A regional program wants to know whether a survey result closely represents the health state the survey is intended to measure. Which property is the program assessing?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Validity is how closely a measurement corresponds to the state it is intended to measure.

distractor_rationales.B: Reliability concerns reproducibility rather than correspondence to the intended state.
distractor_rationales.C: Incidence concerns new events over time.
distractor_rationales.D: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is identified when appraising research.

items.stem: A health team confirms that its assessment tool is reproducible but has not assessed whether the tool corresponds to the health state it is intended to measure. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The tool is valid because it is reproducible.
The tool is reliable, but validity has not been established.
The tool identifies the study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Reproducibility supports reliability; reliability alone does not establish validity.

distractor_rationales.A: A reproducible measurement can still be invalid.
distractor_rationales.B: Incidence is a population-health measure of new events, not a conclusion about reproducibility.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases and is not established by reproducibility.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is a research-appraisal concept, not a conclusion about a tool's reproducibility.

items.stem: A physician reviewing a population-health paper wants to appraise its methods. What should be identified before inferring the study's strengths or limitations?

options.text: The study design and comparison structure
Only the number of existing cases
Only the number of new events

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal should identify the study design; strengths and limitations should not be inferred without identifying the design and comparison structure.

distractor_rationales.B: Existing cases describe prevalence, not the study design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.C: New events describe incidence, not the study design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.D: Reproducibility is reliability of a measurement and does not identify study design.
distractor_rationales.E: Validity is a measurement property and does not identify study design.

items.stem: At journal club, learners compare a randomized trial with observational studies. Which statement best supports a careful appraisal?

options.text: All study designs select, time, and compare participants in the same way.
Study design is irrelevant to critical appraisal.
The designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.
All study designs are measures of incidence.
All study designs are measures of prevalence.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Randomized trials, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, and case-control studies differ in participant selection, timing, and comparison.

distractor_rationales.A: The designs are distinguished by differences in selection, timing, and comparison.
distractor_rationales.B: Critical appraisal should identify the study design.
distractor_rationales.D: Incidence is a measure of new events, not a property of all study designs.
distractor_rationales.E: Prevalence counts existing cases, not a property of all study designs.

items.stem: A public-health resident reads a paper but cannot yet determine whether it is randomized, cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Identify the study design and comparison structure.
Use prevalence to determine the study design.
Use incidence to determine the study design.
Use reliability to determine the study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal should first identify the study design; strengths and limitations should not be inferred without its design and comparison structure.

distractor_rationales.A: The evidence boundary does not support inferring limitations before identifying the design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence is a measure of existing cases, not a way to determine study design.
distractor_rationales.D: Incidence is a measure of new events, not a way to determine study design.
distractor_rationales.E: Reliability is reproducibility of a measurement, not a way to determine study design.

items.stem: A health authority receives reports from a cross-sectional study, a cohort study, and a case-control study. Before comparing their findings, which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Assume the studies have the same comparison structure.
Treat the names of the designs as interchangeable.
Identify how the studies select, time, and compare participants.
Assume all studies measure the same population-health question.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal requires identifying the study design because designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.

distractor_rationales.A: The supported claim is that designs differ in comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.B: The designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.
distractor_rationales.C: Reproducibility addresses reliability of a measurement, not the features distinguishing designs.
distractor_rationales.E: The appropriate first appraisal step is to identify each design and its comparison structure.

items.stem: A public-health physician is reviewing surveillance data to assess how many new events occurred during the past year. Which measure should be used?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Incidence concerns new events occurring over time.

distractor_rationales.B: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.C: Reliability describes reproducibility of a measurement.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity concerns how closely a measurement corresponds to its intended state.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is considered in critical appraisal rather than used as a frequency measure.

items.stem: A health authority is estimating the current burden of a chronic condition to plan ongoing care services. Which measure best answers this question?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population and is useful for estimating chronic-care burden.

distractor_rationales.A: Incidence concerns new events over time rather than existing cases.
distractor_rationales.B: Reliability is reproducibility of a measurement, not a measure of disease burden.
distractor_rationales.C: Validity is a measurement property, not a count of existing cases.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design does not quantify the number of existing cases.

items.stem: A learner says that incidence and prevalence answer the same population-health question. Which correction is most accurate?

options.text: Incidence counts new events over time, whereas prevalence counts existing cases.
Prevalence counts new events over time, whereas incidence counts existing cases.
Both measures assess correspondence to an intended state.
They are alternative names for study design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Incidence concerns new events over time, whereas prevalence counts existing cases in a population.

distractor_rationales.A: Reproducibility describes reliability, not incidence or prevalence.
distractor_rationales.C: This reverses the supported meanings of incidence and prevalence.
distractor_rationales.D: Correspondence to an intended state describes validity.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is distinct from population-health measures.

items.stem: A screening questionnaire gives reproducible results when administered repeatedly under the same conditions. Which measurement property has been demonstrated?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Reliability is the reproducibility of a measurement.

distractor_rationales.A: Incidence is a measure of new events over time.
distractor_rationales.B: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.D: Validity concerns correspondence to the state a measurement is intended to measure.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is not a property of a measurement.

items.stem: A team is evaluating whether an instrument closely corresponds to the health state it was intended to measure. Which property is being assessed?
items.correct_answer_rationale: Validity is how closely a measurement corresponds to the state it is intended to measure.

distractor_rationales.A: Reliability concerns reproducibility rather than correspondence to the intended state.
distractor_rationales.B: Incidence concerns new events over time.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases in a population.
distractor_rationales.D: Study design is not a measurement property.

items.stem: A measurement is shown to be reproducible, but there is no evidence about how closely it represents the intended health state. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: It is valid because it is reproducible.
It is reliable, but validity has not been established.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Reproducibility supports reliability, but reliability alone does not establish validity.

distractor_rationales.A: A reproducible measurement can still be invalid.
distractor_rationales.C: Incidence is a population-health measure of new events, not a conclusion from reproducibility.
distractor_rationales.D: Prevalence counts existing cases and is not established by reproducibility.
distractor_rationales.E: Study design is unrelated to whether a measurement is reproducible.

items.stem: A resident begins to appraise a population-health study. Before drawing conclusions about the study's strengths or limitations, what is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Identify the study design and comparison structure.
Assume its strengths from the reported results.
Use prevalence to classify the design.
Use incidence to classify the design.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal should identify the study design; strengths and limitations should not be inferred without its design and comparison structure.

distractor_rationales.B: The evidence boundary does not support inferring strengths before identifying design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.C: Prevalence counts existing cases and does not classify a study design.
distractor_rationales.D: Incidence concerns new events and does not classify a study design.
distractor_rationales.E: Reproducibility is a measurement property and does not identify study design.

items.stem: At a journal club, a physician compares randomized trials, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, and case-control studies. Which statement best supports critical appraisal?

options.text: All designs select, time, and compare participants in the same way.
Study design is irrelevant once results are reported.
The designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.
All designs are measures of incidence.
All designs are measures of prevalence.

items.correct_answer_rationale: These study designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared, so design must be identified during critical appraisal.

distractor_rationales.A: The supported claim is that the designs differ in selection, timing, and comparison.
distractor_rationales.B: Critical appraisal should identify the study design.
distractor_rationales.D: Incidence is a measure of new events, not a characteristic of all study designs.
distractor_rationales.E: Prevalence counts existing cases, not a characteristic of all study designs.

items.stem: A clinician reads a paper but cannot determine whether its design is randomized, cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control. What should the clinician do next?

options.text: Treat the named designs as interchangeable.
Determine the number of existing cases only.
Identify the study design and comparison structure.
Determine whether the measurement is reproducible only.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Critical appraisal should first identify the study design and comparison structure before inferring strengths or limitations.

distractor_rationales.A: The evidence boundary says not to infer limitations before identifying design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.B: The designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared.
distractor_rationales.C: Existing cases describe prevalence, not the design and comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.E: Reproducibility concerns reliability of a measurement, not the study design.

items.stem: A health authority receives findings from several population-health studies and plans to compare them. Which approach is most appropriate before interpreting their differences?

options.text: Assume all studies use the same comparison structure.
Identify how each study selects, times, and compares participants.
Assume all study designs answer the same question.
Compare only the prevalence reported by each study.
Compare only the reliability of measurements.

items.correct_answer_rationale: Study designs differ in how participants are selected, timed, and compared; identifying those features is required for critical appraisal.

distractor_rationales.A: The supported claim is that designs differ in comparison structure.
distractor_rationales.C: The study designs are not interchangeable for critical appraisal.
distractor_rationales.D: Prevalence is a measure of existing cases and does not identify the relevant design features.
distractor_rationales.E: Reliability concerns measurement reproducibility, not the features that distinguish study designs.
